interactions.summary: Jiang continues his answer on schooling by arguing that both private and public schools no longer teach children to read, write, or think independently. He says contemporary schools mainly deliver ideological programming rather than intellectual formation, which is why he sees no remaining relevance for public education.

The host asks whether civilizations learn from repeated cycles of glut, growth, and collapse, and whether China's repeated dynastic experience offers lessons for industrial-civilization breakdown. Jiang answers through Spengler that civilizations are supposed to die, and that collapse often releases creativity and new political forms. He treats Western renewal after prior collapses as a strength, but says China has persisted too long because geography, scale, and inertia keep it alive past its productive time.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Host question followed by Jiang answer

interactions.summary: The host asks whether Jiang's bleak view of Chinese civilization makes life in China personally dangerous or difficult, and questions whether outside stories about Chinese authoritarianism match daily experience. Jiang replies that ordinary people who do not fight for money or power are mostly ignored. He explains that he chose not to use his Yale and education-world connections during the 2008 boom to become rich, because doing so would have made him dependent on officials, investors, and partners. He frames that refusal as a tradeoff in favor of creativity and intellectual independence, and says staying in China as a normal person has served that goal better than returning to Canada, the United States, or Australia.

claims.claim: Jiang argues that contemporary schools, including private schools, no longer teach children to read books, write essays, or think for themselves, and instead mainly deliver ideological content and passive social conditioning.
Jiang says public schools no longer have real relevance because they fail at intellectual formation and instead reproduce compliant attitudes.
Drawing on Spengler, Jiang argues that civilizations are meant to be born, rise, and die, and that civilizational death is not only normal but often necessary for renewal.
Jiang argues that Western civilization became innovative because earlier civilizational collapses cleared space for new societies to learn from older failures and adapt to new circumstances.

Jiang uses the Bronze Age collapse as an example of destruction generating new creativity, linking it to the rise of the Greek polis and, through Egyptian decline, to the Davidic kingdom that gave rise to the Bible.

Jiang says China has endured too long because geography, scale, and inertia have preserved it past its productive civilizational phase, and he concludes that it eventually needs to disappear so innovation can flourish.
Jiang describes Chinese social logic as a zero-sum competition for power pursued mainly to obtain wealth, with people outside that competition treated as weak or irrelevant rather than threatening.

Jiang says he deliberately refused obvious wealth-making opportunities during China's 2008 education boom because becoming rich would have required dependence on investors, officials, and business partners, costing him intellectual independence.
claims.temporal_scope: Autobiographical retrospective stated on 2025-12-31 about choices beginning around 2008.

claims.claim: Jiang argues that, for him, remaining a normal person in China has preserved creativity and intellectual freedom better than life in Canada, the United States, or Australia would have.

signature_moments.moment: School is recast as a place where children are present but not actually being taught how to think.
signature_moments.source_phrase: kids don't learn anything in school
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the sharp public-school culmination of the prior packet's nation-state myth argument, stripping schooling down to empty attendance plus ideology.

signature_moments.moment: Civilizational death is treated not as tragedy alone but as the precondition for human creativity and political rebirth.
signature_moments.source_phrase: all civilizations, they should die at some point
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's governing reversal: collapse is not merely failure but the mechanism by which new forms become possible.

signature_moments.moment: China is described as a civilization that has outlived its useful historical time.
signature_moments.source_phrase: it's been around for like too long
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The line radicalizes Jiang's cyclical theory by applying it directly to China rather than only to the modern West.

signature_moments.moment: Success is turned into captivity because wealth-making binds the thinker to the very system he wants to stay free from.
signature_moments.source_phrase: I would surrender my freedom to think for myself
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This gives Jiang's personal China answer its core paradox: opting out of ambition is what preserves agency.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Invoked by Jiang as the cyclical theorist whose model treats civilizations like living organisms that are born, flourish, and die.
Used by Jiang as an example of systemic breakdown that cleared the way for later political creativity, including the Greek polis and biblical civilization.
Jiang's example of a new political form that emerged after civilizational collapse and became foundational for later Western development.
A phrase crystallizing Jiang's view that financial and career success can trap a person inside dependence networks that destroy intellectual freedom.

chronology_notes.note: On 2025-12-31 Jiang pushes his schooling-as-brainwashing thesis beyond legitimacy maintenance into a broader late-2025 claim that contemporary schools no longer perform serious intellectual education at all.

This late-2025 interview records Jiang applying a Spenglerian rise-and-death model directly to China, not just to Western decline, and treating civilizational disappearance as a condition of renewal rather than merely a loss to prevent.

Jiang anchors his China-versus-West freedom comparison in an autobiographical timeline that includes nearly 30 years in China and a conscious refusal, beginning around the 2008 boom, to convert educational and overseas connections into wealth.

uncertainty_notes.note: The packet records Jiang's sweeping school critique as his polemical late-2025 judgment about present education, not as an independently measured assessment of classroom outcomes across systems.

Jiang's Bronze Age, Greek polis, and Davidic-kingdom chain is presented as a compressed civilizational interpretation inside the interview rather than a step-by-step historical argument defended with sources in this packet.

The 2008 education-boom and wealth-foregoing material is autobiographical self-report, and the ASR is rough around some business details, so the packet preserves the freedom-versus-success tradeoff without over-normalizing every garbled phrase.
